newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- DEC 3.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- DEC 3.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:
KATHIMERINI

--The continuing blockade of national roads by protesting farmers and the seventh strike day at the nation's ports is causing major problems for exports and the operating needs of firms. The difficulties are being reflected in the market for fresh produce and dairy products, facilitating a rise in prices and profiteering.

--Yesterday's Treasury bill offer was greeted with a massive demand, leading to queues and delays in transactions. The finance ministry's final issue for the year will see a further reduction in interest rates to 11.25 percent as it appears that demand has been piqued by the taxation of state titles as of the new year.
--Financial houses Ernst & Young, Deloitte & Touche and Peat Marwick will proceed with an exhaustive inspection of all stock and bond holdings of all brokerage firms, possibly tomorrow.
--A recent Bank of Greece decision has paved the way for ETBA to expand its activities and become more of a commercial bank, excluding, however, housing lending and consumer credit.
IMERISIA

--The farmers' blockade is choking off the life supply for firms and paralysing the country's economic and social life. The recent bad weather failed to thwart the determination of the farmers who have rejected a proposal by Agriculture Minister Stephanos Tzoumakas to meet. Farmers demand a meeting with Prime Minister Costas Simitis as they continue setting new blocks.
--The government insists on talks with the farmers but there are signs that its position will harden while opposition parties support the protestors.
--Tomorrow is the finance ministry's deadline for debtors to the state to resettle outstanding debts with favourable terms. This deadline is the second extension so far.
--Twenty-four public utilities and organisations will begin their search for managers from the private sector in January, according to reports.
KERDOS

--The agriculture ministry's proposals have fallen on deaf ears as the protest appears to expand. By late last night there had been no meeting between the government and the strikers, while the protestors found little joy in statements by minister Tzoumakas.
--First estimates put yesterday's offer of state titles at 450 billion drachmas, an encouraging return for Treasury bills with significantly reduced interest rates.
--The government's new bill on taxation measures will be submitted to Parliament today along with any fine tuning.
EXPRESS

--The blockade has reached a dangerous impasse with companies caught in the middle. The government's latest effort to satisfy the protestors without harm to the economy has come to naught. Realising the farmers' demands would cost one trillion drachmas.
--The government will release a list of major tax evaders by the end of the week, according to reports. The list is expected to include 'audacious' and 'provocative' cases of tax evasion.
NAFTEMBORIKI
--The paralysis of the country's ports has dealt the final blow to the market. Some 7,500 containers destined for the main port of Piraeus have ended up at other ports in the eastern Mediterranean.

--The majority of Greek businessmen have a negative opinion on the role of the state in the development of business activity, according to a new study. The study has been conducted on the occasion of tonight's 'Kouros 1996' awards for the most outstanding new Greek businessmen or women. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
